'''Richard Anthony Jefferson''' (born 1956) is an American-born [[molecular biologist]] and [[social entrepreneur]] who developed the widely used [[GUS reporter system|reporter gene system GUS]],<ref name="gus"/> conducted the world's first biotech crop release, proposed the [[Hologenome theory of evolution]], pioneered [[Biological Innovation for Open Society|Biological Open Source]] and founded [[The Lens]]. He is founder of the social enterprise [[CAMBIA|Cambia]] and a professor of Biological Innovation at the [[Queensland University of Technology]]. In 2003, he was named by [[Scientific American]] as one of the world's 50 most influential technologists, and is renowned for his work on making science-enabled innovation more widely accessible.<ref>Scientific American Website: The 2003 Scientific American 50 List of Winners [http://www.sciam.com/article.cfm?articleID=000E18BE-3623-1FAC-B62383414B7F0000] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071013165951/http://www.sciam.com/article.cfm?articleID=000E18BE-3623-1FAC-B62383414B7F0000|date=13 October 2007}}, URL accessed on 30 May 2006</ref><ref name="googlescholar">{{GoogleScholar|VVJ_j-cAAAAJ}}</ref> He was profiled in 'Open & Shut: The Basement Interviews',<ref>{{Cite web|url = http://poynder.blogspot.com/2006/09/interview-with-richard-jefferson.html|title = Open and Shut?: Interview with Richard Jefferson|date = 22 September 2006|access-date = 23 July 2015|archive-date = 24 July 2015|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20150724040331/http://poynder.blogspot.com/2006/09/interview-with-richard-jefferson.html|url-status = live}}</ref> and other major media, including in an Economist Feature 'Grassroots Innovator' in 2001.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.economist.com/technology-quarterly/2001/12/08/grassroots-innovator|title=Grassroots innovator|newspaper=The Economist|date=8 December 2001|access-date=6 August 2015|archive-date=8 September 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150908020751/http://www.economist.com/node/885178|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Education ==

Born in [[Santa Cruz, California|Santa Cruz]], [[California]], Jefferson studied at the [[University of California, Santa Barbara]] at the [[College of Creative Studies]], and obtained his BA (Molecular Genetics) in 1978. He then moved to the [[University of Colorado Boulder]] for his [[Ph.D.]], where he first developed the GUS reporter system, isolating, sequencing and characterizing the first microbial glucuronidase,<ref name="gus"/><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Jefferson | first1 = R. A. | last2 = Burgess | first2 = S. M. | last3 = Hirsh | first3 = D. | year = 1986 | title = Beta-Glucuronidase from ''Escherichia Coli'' as a Gene-Fusion Marker | journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences | volume = 83 | issue = 22| pages = 8447–8451 | doi = 10.1073/pnas.83.22.8447 | pmid=3534890 | pmc=386947| bibcode = 1986PNAS...83.8447J | doi-access = free }}</ref> and creating transgenic technology for [[Caenorhabditis elegans]]<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Jefferson | first1 = Richard A. | last2 = Klass | first2 = Michael | last3 = Wolf | first3 = Nurit | last4 = Hirsh | first4 = David | year = 1987 | title = Expression of Chimeric Genes in ''Caenorhabditis Elegans'' | journal = Journal of Molecular Biology | volume = 193 | issue = 1| pages = 41–46 | doi = 10.1016/0022-2836(87)90624-3 | pmid = 3295256 }}</ref>

==Career==

As a [[postdoctoral research]]er he worked at the [[John Innes Centre|Plant Breeding Institute]] in [[Cambridge]], [[England]]: there he adapted the GUS assay for the use in plants.<ref name="gus">{{Cite journal
 | pmid = 3327686
| year = 1987
| last1 = Jefferson
| first1 = R. A.
| author-link1 = Richard Anthony Jefferson
| title = GUS fusions: Beta-glucuronidase as a sensitive and versatile gene fusion marker in higher plants
| journal = The EMBO Journal
| volume = 6
| issue = 13
| pages = 3901–7
| last2 = Kavanagh
| first2 = T. A.
| last3 = Bevan
| first3 = M. W.
| author-link3 = Michael W. Bevan
| pmc = 553867
 | doi=10.1002/j.1460-2075.1987.tb02730.x
}}</ref> His GUS system was a breakthrough in plant molecular sciences, useful for the development of efficient transformation methods for crop plants, and cell and developmental biology. In 1986-87, he sent all the components of the GUS system (DNA and strains) together with a comprehensive users' manual to nearly a thousand labs worldwide, before publication, pioneering a biological open source paradigm and a rapid uptake of the technology.   The GUS system and its novel mode of dissemination was said to be essential for development of transformation of the most important crops, including soybean, maize, cotton and rice. The work has been cited in the primary literature almost 15,000 times,<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://scholar.google.com.au/citations?user=VVJ_j-cAAAAJ&hl=en |title=Richard Anthony Jefferson - Google Scholar Citations |access-date=2015-07-23 |archive-date=2015-07-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150724030654/https://scholar.google.com.au/citations?user=VVJ_j-cAAAAJ&hl=en |url-status=dead }}</ref> and has been licensed by every major company in crop genetics.

During his postdoc in [[Cambridge]], he also initiated and managed, with his colleague [[Michael W. Bevan]], the world's first field release of a [[transgenic plants|transgenic food crop]] (June 1, 1987), in Trumpington, near Cambridge, UK.<ref name="multiple">{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1162/itgg.2006.1.4.13| title = Science as Social Enterprise: The CAMBIA BiOS Initiative| journal = Innovations: Technology, Governance, Globalization| volume = 1| issue = 4| pages = 13–44| year = 2006| last1 = Jefferson| first1 = R.| s2cid = 57559694| url = https://ses.library.usyd.edu.au/bitstream/2123/2686/1/LegalFramework_Ch18.pdf| doi-access = free| access-date = 26 October 2018| archive-date = 13 August 2017| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20170813164434/https://ses.library.usyd.edu.au/bitstream/2123/2686/1/LegalFramework_Ch18.pdf| url-status = live}}</ref><ref>Jefferson, Richard A. "New Approaches for Agricultural Molecular Biology: From Single Cells to Field Analysis." Stadler Genetics Symposia Series (1990): 365–400. doi:10.1007/978-1-4684-7047-5_20.</ref> The planting date of the experiment was serendipitously one day before that of Monsanto, in Jerseyville, Illinois, which has been widely but incorrectly viewed as the first such trial.<ref>{{Cite web | year=2001 | author1=E Simanis | author2=S. Hart | publisher=World Resources Institute Case Study | url=http://pdf.wri.org/bell/case_1-56973-475-5_full_version_a_english.pdf | title=The Monsanto Company: Quest for Sustainability (A) | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210205060953/http://pdf.wri.org/bell/case_1-56973-475-5_full_version_a_english.pdf | archive-date=5 February 2021 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | title=Archives of the Office of Technology Assessment (OTA) | url=https://www.princeton.edu/~ota/disk2/1988/8816/881609.PDF | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305014804/https://www.princeton.edu/~ota/disk2/1988/8816/881609.PDF | archive-date=5 March 2016 }}</ref>

In 1989, driven by a need to see the tools of science more broadly accessible and more effectively used in complex environments, Jefferson joined the [[Food and Agriculture Organization|Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)]] as senior scientist, the first molecular biologist in this position. Since then he traveled, worked and taught in many [[developing countries]]. He left the organization in 1991 to start a non-profit private [[social enterprise]], [[CAMBIA|Cambia]].  Cambia soon moved to [[Australia]], due to Jefferson's involvement in the Asian [[rice]] [[biotechnology]] programs of the [[Rockefeller Foundation]],<ref name="multiple"/> and the proximity to almost half the world's agricultural population.

In September 1994, Jefferson first articulated the Hologenome Theory of Evolution, at a presentation at [[Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory]], at a Symposium "A Decade of PCR"<ref>Number 6 in a series of 7 VHS recordings, 'A Decade of PCR: Celebrating 10 Years of Amplification,' released by Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Press, 1994. {{ISBN|0-87969-473-4}}.</ref> This theory was developed from his molecular and genetic work on glucuronide metabolism by vertebrate-associated microbes, including the role of glucuronidases, sulfatases and other enzymes in modulating and effecting [[enterohepatic circulation]] of [[steroid hormones]]. The levels, ratios and timing of steroid hormone de-conjugation (activation) and resorption modulates virtually all aspects of vertebrate ontogeny, physiology and reproduction. The premise for his theory was that natural selection acts on the [[holobiont]] comprising a 'scaffold genome' and myriad microbial constituents in diverse ecosystems, selecting for persistence of the set of genetically encoded capabilities.

In January 1997, the hologenome theory was extended, informed by further work on the molecular genetics of enteric microbial glucuronide metabolism, to emphasize the central role of microbially-mediated hormone modulation (MHM) as an essential component of multi-cellularity and vertebrate biology. This led Jefferson to coin the term ecotherapeutics, or ecological therapeutics, stating that a major route to improved performance or health of animals or plants would be through the adjustment of microbial populations and their genetic capabilities ([[microbiota]], often now called the microbiomes).<ref>Jefferson, Richard A et al.. (1997). Molecular genetics of the ''E. coli gus'' operon: Medical and evolutionary implications for glucuronide and xenobiotic metabolism. 14th Congress of the South African Society of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology in Grahamstown, South Africa. Zenodo. 10.5281/zenodo.22796</ref>

The development of theory and its logic were also outlined in detail in his blog in 2007,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://blogs.cambia.org/raj/2007/09/06/the-hologenome-hologenomics/ |title=The Hologenome & Hologenomics: A different lens on evolution – Science as Social Enterprise |access-date=2015-07-23 |archive-date=2011-07-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110715103611/http://blogs.cambia.org/raj/2007/09/06/the-hologenome-hologenomics/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> and summarized in a cover article Jan 9, 2013, by Carrie Arnold in New Scientist<ref>{{cite journal | doi = 10.1016/s0262-4079(13)60115-3 | bibcode=2013NewSc.217...30A | volume=217 | issue=2899 | title=The hologenome: A new view of evolution | journal=New Scientist | pages=30–34| year=2013 | last1=Arnold | first1=Carrie }}</ref>

In 1999, Jefferson was appointed as Author-in-Chief to the United Nations [[Convention on Biological Diversity]] for the landmark study, submitted to the UN General Assembly, on the contentious genetic technology, colloquially called 'Terminator Technology'. In this study,<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.cbd.int/doc/meetings/sbstta/sbstta-04/official/sbstta-04-09-rev1-en.pdf | title=Consequences of the use of the new technology for the control of plant gene expression for the conservation and sustainable use of biological diversity | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304111536/https://www.cbd.int/doc/meetings/sbstta/sbstta-04/official/sbstta-04-09-rev1-en.pdf |archive-date=4 March 2016 }}</ref> he coined and defined the term GURT - [[Genetic Use Restriction Technology]] and its variants.

At Cambia, and with the initial funding and partnership with Rockefeller Foundation's agriculture program, Jefferson and the Cambia staff started to develop key new tools - including the {{Not a typo|pCambia}} vectors,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.researchgate.net/post/Why_do_most_of_the_people_select_pCambia_vectors_for_cloning_in_transgenic_plants|title=Why do most of the people select pCambia vectors for cloning in transgenic plants?|access-date=3 December 2017|archive-date=9 November 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151109044049/http://www.researchgate.net/post/Why_do_most_of_the_people_select_pCambia_vectors_for_cloning_in_transgenic_plants|url-status=live}}</ref> released in 1997, and which now are the most widely used plasmids in plant biotechnology.

The continuous distribution of thousands of these tools without restrictions throughout the world, the dozens of conducted training courses, and the newly invented open technologies advanced what would become the [[Biological Open Source]] initiative, formally launched in 2005. That year, Jefferson and colleagues published a landmark paper in ''Nature'',<ref>Broothaerts, Wim, Heidi J. Mitchell, Brian Weir, Sarah Kaines, Leon M. A. Smith, Wei Yang, Jorge E. Mayer, Carolina Roa-Rodríguez, and Richard A. Jefferson. "Gene Transfer to Plants by Diverse Species of Bacteria." Nature 433, no. 7026 (February 10, 2005): 629–633. doi:10.1038/nature03309.</ref> in which they described a new biological open source invention, ''TransBacter''.

''Agrobacterium''-mediated gene transfer was by far the most common tool for agricultural biotechnology, but due to complex and extensive patenting, and aggressive pursuit of dominant patents by Monsanto, the use of the tool was constrained to merely academic pursuits or by use of multinational corporations under license. Using [[Patent Lens]] - the most popular global open full-text patent search engine - founded by Jefferson and his colleague Carol Nottenburg in 1999 as CambiaIP Resource - Cambia published the world's first open patent landscape.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.cambia.org/daisy/AgroTran/835.html |title=Agrobacterium-mediated transformation |access-date=2015-08-06 |archive-date=2015-07-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150719034208/http://www.cambia.org/daisy/AgroTran/835.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> Using the evidence and clarity obtained from this patent landscape, Jefferson and his colleagues designed and created an effective alternative technology that would not be constrained by any of the existing patents (of which there were by then almost a thousand). The technology, called ''Transbacter'' involved using three taxes of benign plant-associated bacteria modified with the gene-transfer components from ''Agrobacterium'', to efficiently transfer genes to diverse crop species. "Transbacter" was made available under the first BiOS (Biological Open Source) license, for free to anyone and sent to hundreds of labs worldwide, and was licensed by public sector, small enterprise and multinationals under open principles, with commitments to share improvements with other licensees. The open patent landscape, initially authored by patent experts Nottenburg and Carolina Roa-Rodriguez and later updated by several other Cambia staff, in addition to many other landscapes serve as prototypes of Jefferson's subsequent initiative; open ''Innovation Cartography''<ref>{{Cite web|url = http://grist.org/food/a-16th-century-dutchman-can-tell-us-everything-we-need-to-know-about-gmo-patents/|title = A 16th-century Dutchman can tell us everything we need to know about GMO patents|date = 28 October 2013|access-date = 7 August 2015|archive-date = 7 September 2015|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20150907001631/http://grist.org/food/a-16th-century-dutchman-can-tell-us-everything-we-need-to-know-about-gmo-patents/|url-status = live}}</ref>

In 2009, with funding from the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, The Lemelson Foundation and the Gordon & Betty Moore Foundation, Jefferson moved with part of Cambia to the [[Queensland University of Technology]] (QUT) in Brisbane, Australia, as Professor of Science, Technology & Law, to direct the global activities on open ''Innovation Cartography''.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://blogs.cambia.org/raj/2011/01/10/innovation-cartography-mapping-and-navigating-the-landscape/ |title=Innovation cartography: Mapping and navigating the IP landscape - Science as Social Enterprise |access-date=2015-07-23 |archive-date=2012-03-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120317071907/http://blogs.cambia.org/raj/2011/01/10/innovation-cartography-mapping-and-navigating-the-landscape/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Known also for his expertise in [[intellectual property]], Jefferson remains active in the promotion of [[Open-source model|open source]] biological innovation which has been covered extensively by global media.<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1038/nbt0605-643| title = Profile: Richard Jefferson| journal = Nature Biotechnology| volume = 23| issue = 6| pages = 643| year = 2005| last1 = Herrera | first1 = S. | s2cid = 40766547| doi-access = free}}</ref> He served on the World Economic Forum's Global Agenda Council on Intellectual Property for four years, and is on the WEF's Global Agenda Council on the Economics of Innovation. In 2013, Cambia launched The Lens<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.lens.org/ |title=Home |website=lens.org |access-date=8 August 2022 |archive-date=5 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220805083325/https://www.lens.org/ |url-status=live }}</ref> to replace the older [[Patent Lens]] and enable broader innovation-focused navigation platforms. Jefferson is considered a global leader in social entrepreneurship and is an Outstanding Social Entrepreneur of the Schwab Foundation,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.schwabfound.org/sf/SocialEntrepreneurs/Profiles/index.htm?sname=129191|title=Schwab Foundation for Social Entrepreneurship|website=www.schwabfound.org | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140409015544/http://www.schwabfound.org/entrepreneurs?sname=129191 | archive-date=2014-04-09}}</ref> and a plenary speaker at the Skoll World Forum.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://skollworldforum.org/contributor/richard-jefferson/|title=Skoll1 &#124; Skoll World Forum|access-date=24 July 2015|archive-date=18 May 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150518151456/https://skollworldforum.org/contributor/richard-jefferson/|url-status=live}}</ref> Jefferson was also a keynote speaker at Consilience 2016, organised by [[National Law School of India University]], [[Bengaluru]] on Intellectual Property and the Commons.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.consilience-nls.com/ |title=Consilience 16 &#124; A conference on open access and IP |access-date=16 February 2017 |archive-date=22 October 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161022000436/http://www.consilience-nls.com/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>
